python-sebae.summary: A large, nonvenomous constrictor introduced to southern Florida. African rock pythons can resemble Burmese pythons, so a photograph and expert identification are more useful than a guess from size alone. Keep your distance from any large unfamiliar snake.

sources.label: Florida Museum · African rock python

senna-didymobotrya.summary: Often sold as popcorn cassia, this African shrub gets its nickname from the scent of its rubbed foliage. It grows quickly and can become a small tree in warm climates, while gardeners in colder regions often grow it as a seasonal ornamental.

sources.label: University of Wisconsin Extension

tamarix-africana.summary: This tamarisk carries exceptionally small leaves: individual blades are only about 1.5–2.5 millimeters long. Identifying a tamarisk to species takes more than its feathery appearance; retain close photographs of leaves and flowers for comparison with a botanical key.

sources.label: Flora of North America

spathodea-campanulata.summary: Large orange-red flowers with crinkled yellow edges make African tulip trees easy to notice. Long capsules split to release light, winged seeds, and damaged trees can produce root suckers. In tropical and subtropical regions it can spread beyond planted landscapes into wetter disturbed habitats.

sources.label: Environmental Weeds of Australia · Botanical key

phacochoerus-africanus.summary: The familiar warthog has a large head, curved tusks and a mane along its back. It often lowers itself onto its padded wrist joints to graze and uses its snout and tusks to dig for underground plant parts. These traits describe the animal; a catalog entry alone does not establish a wild population near you.

sources.label: University of Michigan · Animal Diversity Web

dioscorea-bulbifera.summary: Air potato is a climbing vine with broad, heart-shaped leaves and potato-like bulbils held above ground along its stems. Those bulbils are a useful recognition clue. In Florida, vines can climb into tree canopies, so look up as well as along fences and woodland edges.

sources.label: University of Florida · Air potato

melampsoridium-hiratsukanum.summary: Alder rust can leave orange-yellow pustules beneath alder leaves, with yellow or orange spots above. Leaves may curl, brown or fall early. Several alder rust fungi look alike, so these symptoms justify closer examination rather than a species-level diagnosis from a photograph.

sources.label: California Department of Food and Agriculture

pinus-halepensis.summary: Aleppo pine usually has thin, light-green needles in pairs and an irregular crown that broadens with age. Its cones can remain attached for years. Native to the Mediterranean, it is widely grown in California and the Southwest, where a planted tree should not be confused with evidence of an invading population.

sources.label: Oregon State University · Landscape Plants

ptychosperma-elegans.summary: Also called solitaire palm, this Australian palm has a single slim, pale trunk marked with rings. Look for jagged, squared-off leaflet tips, a smooth green crownshaft and bright red fruit. Despite the common name Alexander palm, the scientific name matters when comparing it with other ornamental palms.

sources.label: University of Florida · Solitaire palm

calophyllum-inophyllum.summary: Glossy oval leaves, fragrant white flowers and round green fruits distinguish this tropical tree, also called beauty leaf or tamanu. Numerous fine veins run from the leaf's central rib toward its edges. It is often planted ornamentally, so nearby seedlings and the original landscape tree provide different kinds of evidence.

sources.label: Singapore National Parks · Flora & Fauna Web
National Tropical Botanical Garden

medicago-sativa.summary: Alfalfa is a long-lived forage legume grown for hay and livestock feed. Its deep root system helps it tolerate dry conditions, and its flowers commonly appear purple. Finding it beyond a field is worth documenting, but its importance as a crop should be distinguished from its behavior in a particular natural habitat.

sources.label: University of Minnesota Extension · Forage legumes
University of Minnesota Extension · Alfalfa flowers

medicago-sativa-ssp-sativa.summary: This entry represents a subspecies of alfalfa rather than a separate, unrelated plant. Alfalfa is a perennial forage legume; purple-flowered forms are familiar in fields and along their edges. Keep the subspecies name attached to a record only when its source supports that more precise identification.

sources.label: University of Minnesota Extension · Alfalfa flower variation

gracilaria-vermiculophylla.summary: This branching red seaweed can form bushy tangles of narrow, cylindrical strands. Its color ranges from reddish brown to greenish or nearly black, making color an unreliable shortcut. Closely related seaweeds look similar; reliable identification can require microscopy or genetic analysis.

sources.label: Smithsonian Environmental Research Center · NEMESIS

grateloupia-doryphora.summary: Use this name carefully when reading older seaweed records. Large red algae introduced to Europe and New England were once called Grateloupia doryphora, but genetic work identified them as G. turuturu. A historical label should therefore be checked before transferring its distribution or impacts to this species.

sources.label: Smithsonian Environmental Research Center · Identification history

limonium-ramosissimum.summary: Algerian sea lavender is a management concern in San Francisco Bay tidal marshes. It is easily confused with European sea lavender, so photographs alone may not settle an identification. The distinction matters when recording a patch, comparing older surveys or planning work around sensitive marsh habitat.

sources.label: California Invasive Plant Council · Sea lavender research
Cal-IPC · Similar-species caution

alternanthera-philoxeroides.summary: Alligatorweed spreads across water and wet banks on sprawling stems. Look for opposite leaves and small, white, papery flower heads held on stalks; aquatic stems are often hollow. Stem fragments can root, which is why broken pieces deserve attention when cleaning equipment or moving plant material.

sources.label: University of Florida · Alligatorweed
University of Florida IFAS · Weed management

phytomyza-gymnostoma.summary: Rows of tiny white punctures on onion, leek or garlic leaves are an early clue to allium leafminer activity. Adult females make the marks, while larvae feed inside the plant. Photograph both the damaged leaf and the whole crop before seeking confirmation, since not every damaged onion has this pest.

sources.label: Penn State Extension · Allium leafminer

pimenta-dioica.summary: Allspice comes from the dried, unripe berries of this tropical tree, rather than a mixture of spices. Its native range includes southern Mexico, Central America and parts of the Caribbean. A familiar culinary use does not tell us how a tree behaves outside cultivation in a particular place.

sources.label: Indian Institute of Spices Research · Allspice
Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

cadra-cautella.summary: Almond moth is a stored-food pest whose larvae can infest bagged grain and the surface of bulk grain stores. The name is narrower than its food supply: an infestation is not limited to almonds. When moths appear around stored food, identifying the infested product is as important as identifying the adult.

sources.label: Canadian Grain Commission · Almond moth

aloephagus-myersi.summary: Tiny aloe aphids can hide beneath leaf bases, where their fluffy wax may be more visible than their bodies. Wingless adults are roughly 2 millimeters long and may be attended by ants. Inspect sheltered parts of an aloe rather than only its exposed leaf surfaces.

sources.label: Blackman & Eastop · Aphids on the World's Plants

trifolium-hybridum.summary: Alsike clover has white-to-pink flower heads and smooth leaflets without the pale watermark often seen on other clovers. It favors moist ground and can reseed into pastures and roadsides. Despite its scientific name, it is a distinct species, not a hybrid of red and white clover.

sources.label: University of Minnesota Extension · Forage legumes

alyssum-strigosum.summary: An annual alyssum native from southern Europe toward Afghanistan. Its name needs particular care in North American records: Flora of North America notes that many reports were based on misidentified A. simplex. Check the specimen or original identification before treating an old record as confirmed.

sources.label: Flora of North America · Alyssum identification notes
Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

aphis-amaranthi.summary: Amaranth aphids are small olive-green or reddish-brown insects associated with amaranths. Colonies can occur around roots and stem bases as well as leaves and flower clusters, and ants often attend them. A close look near the base of a plant may reveal insects missed by a quick leaf check.

sources.label: Blackman & Eastop · Aphids on the World's Plants

pterygoplichthys-pardalis.summary: An armored suckermouth catfish often called an Amazon sailfin catfish. Dark markings on its underside help distinguish it from related species, but the patterns can vary and should not be used alone. Several similar aquarium catfishes have been introduced outside their native range, making careful identification important.

sources.label: US Army Corps of Engineers · Suckermouth catfishes

cecropia-pachystachya.summary: Ambay pumpwood is a tropical South American tree, native from Brazil to northeastern Argentina. It belongs to a genus containing several similar trees, so a general identification as Cecropia is not automatically an identification of this species. Check the scientific name attached to a photograph or occurrence record.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · Plants of the World Online

anisandrus-maiche.summary: This small ambrosia beetle was documented in North America in research published in 2009. Like other ambrosia beetles, it bores into woody hosts and is associated with fungi. Tiny holes in a tree can have many causes, so the beetle itself and the host's condition are important evidence for identification.

sources.label: USDA Agricultural Research Service · First North American records
